video_caption: The video segment features a series of four static presentation slides against a light green to light orange gradient background. Each slide has a blue rectangular header bar with white text indicating the current topic. The first slide, titled "Formation of Bonds," displays introductory information including "Talk to a Teacher" with a URL (http://spoken-tutorial.org), "National Mission on Education through ICT" with another URL (http://sakshat.ac.in), "Script & Narration: Madhuri Ganapathi," "Animation: Udhaya Chandrika," and "IIT Bombay," dated "27 June 2013." A small black and white logo, representing IIT Bombay, is visible in the bottom right corner. The bottom footer of the screen consistently shows "Madhuri Ganapathi" on the left and "Formation of Bonds" on the right. The second slide, titled "Learning Objectives," lists bullet points: "We will learn to," "Add bonds to the existing bond," "Orient the bonds," "Add Stereochemical bonds," and "Inverse wedge hashes." The third slide, titled "System Requirement," states two bullet points: "Ubuntu Linux OS v 12.04" and "GChemPaint v 0.12.10." The fourth slide, titled "Pre-requisites," advises: "You should be familiar with GChemPaint chemical structure editor" and adds, "If not, for relevant tutorials, please visit http://spoken-tutorial.org." Throughout the segment, the layout, footer, and logo remain consistent as the content of the header and main text changes with each slide.

The video displays a computer application, likely a chemical drawing software, with a white canvas showing the chemical structure "H₃C—CH₃", representing ethane. To the right, a vertical panel serves as a toolbar and properties editor. At the top of this panel are various icons for drawing tools, including a mouse pointer, a pen, a line, an eraser, a text tool ("W"), and different types of bonds and rings. Below these are additional drawing shapes like triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons, octagons, and circles, followed by various arrow types. A "Current element" dropdown is set to "C" (Carbon). Further down, a "Property" and "Value" section shows "Bond length: 207.0" and "Bond angle: 120.0". A checkbox labeled "Merge with existing atoms" is checked. The bottom left of the application window displays "Ready", and the bottom right has a "Help" button. The scene remains static throughout the segment.

The video displays a chemical drawing software interface with a white canvas on the left and a toolbar on the right. Initially, an ethane structure, labeled "H₃C—CH₃," is visible on the canvas. The toolbar features icons for elements like 'C', 'CH₂', 'CH₃', drawing tools (like pen, eraser, bond types), and geometric shapes. Below these, properties like "Bond length" (207.0) and "Bond angle" (120.0) are displayed, along with a "Current element: C" dropdown and a checkbox labeled "Merge with existing atoms." The user first clicks the "Select one or more objects" tool (a white pointer icon) on the toolbar. Then, they click on the existing ethane structure, which highlights it in cyan. After pressing `Ctrl+C` to copy, `Ctrl+V` is pressed twice, causing two more identical ethane structures to appear, initially overlapping each other and the original, all highlighted in cyan. The user then clicks and drags the top cyan-highlighted structure with the mouse, moving it upwards and to the right, separating it from the others. Subsequently, they click and drag another cyan-highlighted structure, moving it to the bottom-right. This action reveals that there are now three distinct ethane structures horizontally arranged on the canvas, all in black text and lines, no longer overlapping. The narrator points out the single bond between the carbon atoms in the structures.

The video segment shows a software interface with a white canvas displaying three identical chemical structures, "H3C—CH3" (ethane). On the right side of the screen, a toolbar is visible, featuring various drawing and editing tools for chemical structures. The "Add a bond or change the multiplicity of an existing one" tool, represented by a bond icon with a slash through it and an 'M' (for multiplicity), is highlighted in the toolbar. A hand-shaped cursor moves over the middle "H3C—CH3" structure and clicks on its single carbon-carbon bond. Upon clicking, the single bond transforms into a double bond, and the hydrogen atoms on the adjacent carbons automatically adjust from "H3C" to "H2C," resulting in the structure "H2C=CH2" (ethene). Simultaneously, a text tooltip appears near the highlighted tool, saying "Add a bond or change the multiplicity of an existing one" in English. Below the tools, a panel shows "Property" and "Value" with "Bond length: 207.0" and "Bond angle: 120.0" displayed. A checkbox for "Merge with existing atoms" is also visible and checked. The overall action demonstrates how to change a single bond to a double bond in a chemical drawing software.

The video shows a computer screen displaying a chemical drawing software. On the left side, a white canvas presents three organic molecules: H3C—CH3, H2C=CH2, and initially another H3C—CH3. On the right, a toolbar with various icons is visible, including drawing tools, bond types, and a properties panel. The properties panel shows "Current element: C" (Carbon), "Bond length: 207.0", and "Bond angle: 120.0", with a checkbox labeled "Merge with existing atoms" (which is checked). The mouse cursor hovers over the single bond of the third H3C—CH3 structure. The speaker instructs to click the existing bond of the third ethane structure twice. Upon the first click, the single bond transforms into a double bond, and the molecule changes from H3C—CH3 to H2C=CH2. After a second click on the same bond, it converts into a triple bond, displaying the molecule as HC≡CH. The speaker then observes that the single bond has been converted to a triple bond and that the number of hydrogen atoms has been reduced from six to two.

The video displays a computer screen with a chemical drawing application open. On the left side of the white canvas, three chemical structures are visible: "H3C—CH3", "H2C═CH2", and "HC≡CH". On the right, a detailed toolbox/palette is shown, featuring drawing tools, bond types, and property settings. At 0:01, the cursor hovers over the "T" icon, which represents the "Add or modify a text tool". At 0:04, the "T" icon is clicked, causing a text formatting panel to appear on the right side of the screen, displaying options for font "Family", "Style", "Underline", and "Position". The speaker then instructs to click below the structures. The cursor moves to the area beneath the first structure, H3C—CH3. Starting from 0:10, the name "Ethane" is typed directly below the first structure, appearing in a green highlighted box. The cursor then moves to the space below the second structure, H2C═CH2, and "Ethene" is typed there, also within a green box at 0:14. Finally, at 0:17, the cursor moves below the third structure, HC≡CH, and "Ethyne" is typed, completing the naming process for the three molecules, each name enclosed in a green box.

The video segment opens with a computer screen displaying a drawing program, likely for chemical structures. On the left side of the white canvas, three chemical structures are visible: H₃C—CH₃ labeled "Ethane", H₂C=CH₂ labeled "Ethene", and HC≡CH labeled "Ethyne". The word "Ethyne" is highlighted with a green rectangle. On the right, a toolbar with various drawing and editing tools is present, along with a properties panel showing "Current element: C" and font options like "Family" and "Style". The speaker instructs the user to press Ctrl+A, and subsequently, all three chemical structures and their labels become highlighted with a light blue border, indicating they are selected. The mouse cursor, a white arrow, then moves to the top-left of the right-side toolbar and hovers over an icon resembling a white arrow. A tooltip appears displaying "Select one or more objects". Following the speaker's instruction to click this tool and drag, the selected structures are then dragged slightly to the left on the canvas before being released, at which point the blue selection borders disappear.

The video segment opens with a static 2D diagram of a "Tetrahedral Methane Structure" displayed on a light green background, with "Structures" in white text at the top left. The diagram shows a central carbon atom (C) bonded to four hydrogen atoms (H). A red arrow indicates a bond length of "1.09 Å" (Angstroms) between a carbon and hydrogen atom. A red arc highlights a bond angle of "109.5°" between two hydrogen atoms and the central carbon atom. At the bottom, white text reads "Madhuri Ganpathi" and "Formation of Bonds". At 0:09, the 2D diagram seamlessly transitions into a 3D animated model of the methane molecule. The model consists of a dark grey spherical carbon atom with a small red "C" label, and four light beige spherical hydrogen atoms, each with a small green "H" label. The molecule rotates slowly, showcasing its tetrahedral geometry. As it rotates, blue arcs appear between different hydrogen atoms and the central carbon atom, each labeled "109.5°", illustrating the equal bond angles within the structure. The background remains a subtle gradient, starting light green at the bottom and transitioning to a light grey-purple at the top.

The video displays a software interface with a large white canvas on the left, currently blank except for three chemical structures labeled "H3C—CH3 Ethane", "H2C═CH2 Ethene", and "HC≡CH Ethyne" at the top. On the right, a vertical toolbar features various icons for drawing and editing. As the narrator instructs, a tooltip appears over the first bond-drawing icon in the toolbar, displaying the text "Add a bond or change the multiplicity of the existing one" (English translation: "Add a bond or change the multiplicity of the existing one"), and the icon is highlighted.

The video displays a computer screen with two main sections. The left section shows a white canvas with chemical structures: "H3C—CH3 Ethane," "H2C=CH2 Ethene," and "HC≡CH Ethyne" at the top. Below these, a skeletal structure of Ethane is depicted with two carbon atoms connected by a single bond, and three hydrogen atoms bonded to each carbon, extending outwards. The right section features a toolbox panel. At the top of this panel are various chemical elements and bond types. The cursor hovers over several bond icons, revealing tooltips: "Add a wedge bond" (0:08), "Add a hash bond" (0:10), "Add a squiggle bond" (0:13), and "Add a fore bond" (0:15). The "Add a wedge bond" icon, represented by a thick triangular line, is then selected (0:25). Below the bond icons, a "Property Value" section is visible, showing "Bond length: 207.0" and "Bond angle: 120.0," along with a checked box for "Merge with existing atoms." The cursor then clicks on various H-C bonds in the Ethane structure on the left pane. Each click cycles the bond type: one bond on the right carbon (0:29) becomes a wedge bond, then a bond on the same carbon (0:30) becomes a hash bond, followed by a bond on the left carbon (0:31) becoming a wedge bond, and another bond on the left carbon (0:32) becoming a hash bond. Subsequently, two of these modified bonds revert to normal single bonds after further clicks (0:33, 0:34). The "Add a wedge bond" icon is clicked again at the end of the segment (0:35).

The video segment displays a software interface, likely a chemical drawing program, with a white canvas on the left and a toolbar/properties panel on the right. On the canvas, three simple chemical structures are shown at the top, labeled "H3C --- CH3 Ethane," "H2C == CH2 Ethene," and "HC === CH Ethyne." Below these, a more complex 3D representation of a molecule resembling ethane is depicted, showing two central atoms bonded together, each connected to three other atoms (implied hydrogen, given the labels). This 3D structure uses solid wedge bonds to indicate atoms coming out of the plane and dashed line bonds for atoms going into the plane. Further down, a simple "H --- H" structure is shown with a hashed (dashed wedge) bond between the two hydrogen atoms, where the narrow end of the wedge is on the left and the broad end is on the right. The right panel, titled "GChemPaint," features various drawing tools at the top (including a cursor, eraser, different bond types, shapes, and text), a "Current element: H" selection, and a "Property" section displaying "Bond length: 207.0" and "Bond angle: 120.0." The "Merge with existing atoms" checkbox is checked. The screen remains static throughout this segment.

The video segment shows a computer screen with a chemical drawing software open. On the left side of the screen, several chemical structures are displayed, including "H3C—CH3 Ethane", "H2C=CH2 Ethene", and a 3D representation of a molecule with a central carbon-carbon bond and six hydrogen atoms attached (three to each carbon). Below this, a single hydrogen atom is shown with a dashed bond to another hydrogen atom (H------H). On the right side, a toolbar and property panel are visible. The mouse cursor, an arrow pointer, moves to the toolbar and clicks on the "Add a hash bond" icon, which looks like a dashed line, causing it to become highlighted. Subsequently, the cursor moves to the 3D chemical structure on the left. It then clicks on three of the carbon-hydrogen bonds on the right side of the molecule, converting each solid line bond into a dashed "hash bond" one by one. The "Current element" in the property panel remains "H" (Hydrogen), and "Bond length" and "Bond angle" values are displayed as "207.0" and "120.0" respectively.

A "Save as" dialog box is prominently displayed on a computer screen. In the upper left corner, the title "Save as" is visible. Below it, there's a text field labeled "Name," which is initially empty. The user types "Formation of bonds" into this field. Beneath the "Name" field, it shows "Save in folder:" with "cdeep" displayed. On the left side of the dialog, a "Places" panel lists various locations such as "Search," "Recently Used," "cdeep," "Desktop," "Documents," "File System," "Music," "Pictures," "Videos," and "Downloads." The main central area of the dialog box shows a list of files and folders within the "cdeep" directory, including "Desktop," "Documents," "Downloads," "Music," "Pictures," and others, along with their modification dates. At the bottom of the dialog, "File type: Automatic" is selected, and two buttons, "Save" (highlighted in orange) and "Cancel," are present. The user then clicks on the "Save" button. Following this action, the "Save as" dialog box closes, revealing a drawing application displaying chemical structures of Ethane, Ethene, Ethyne, and their molecular representations, along with a toolbar on the right side.

The video segment opens with a white and green gradient slide titled "Summary". Bullet points list what has been learned: "Add bonds to the existing bond", "Orient the bonds", "Add Stereochemical bonds", and "Inverse wedge hashes". The bottom of the slide shows "Madhuri Ganpathi" on the left and "Formation of Bonds" with a logo on the right. This transitions to an "Assignment" slide with the same background and footer, presenting three tasks: "1 Convert Propane to Propyne", "2 Draw Propane and butane structures", and "3 Show the stereochemical bonds". The scene then changes to a screenshot of a chemical drawing software interface titled "Stereochemical". On the left side, several chemical structures are displayed, including two representations of "Propane" and one of "Butane". The right side shows a toolbar with various elements and drawing tools, such as 'C', 'CH2', different bond types (single, double, triple), shapes, and arrows. A small "Help" button is visible at the bottom right of the toolbar. The video concludes by showing another slide titled "About the Spoken Tutorial Project", detailing where to "Watch the video available at http://spoken-tutorial.org /What_is_a_Spoken_Tutorial" and stating, "It summarises the Spoken Tutorial project", maintaining the same footer as the previous slides.

The video segment opens at 00:01 with a presentation slide titled "About the Spoken Tutorial Project" against a light green and blue gradient background. The slide displays three bullet points: "Watch the video available at http://spoken-tutorial.org/What_is_a_Spoken_Tutorial", followed by "It summarises the Spoken Tutorial project", and then, appearing at 00:07, "If you do not have good bandwidth, you can download and watch it". At 00:11, the slide transitions to a new one titled "Spoken Tutorial Workshops", maintaining the same background and overall presentation style. This slide presents details about the Spoken Tutorial Project Team, stating they "Conducts workshops using spoken tutorials" and "Gives certificates to those who pass an online test". The final bullet point advises, "For more details, please write to contact@spoken-tutorial.org". Throughout both slides, the name "Madhuri Ganpathi" and the text "Formation of Bonds" are visible in the bottom left corner, while a logo depicting two stylized books is present in the bottom right corner. No people are visible, and there are no significant visual changes other than the slide transition.

The video displays a static presentation slide with a light green and yellow gradient background. The title at the top of the slide reads "Acknowledgements" in dark gray text. Below the title, three bullet points are presented. The first bullet point states, "Spoken Tutorial Project is a part of the Talk to a Teacher project." The second bullet point reads, "It is supported by the National Mission on Education through ICT, MHRD, Government of India." The third bullet point informs, "More information on this Mission is available at http://spoken-tutorial.org /NMEICT-Intro". The URL is highlighted in blue and underlined. At the bottom left of the slide, the name "Madhuri Ganpathi" is displayed, and at the bottom right, the phrase "Formation of Bonds" is visible. A logo featuring the letters "IIT" with a stylized architectural design is positioned in the bottom right corner of the slide. No individuals are visible, and the slide remains unchanged throughout this segment as a voiceover narrates the presented text.
